opus-5.5.text:
I think proof plays a role that people outside mathematics often underestimate. It's not just about being correct. It's about trust, and about making something unfamiliar legible to a community.

When someone discovers something genuinely new, especially something that cuts against intuition or comes from an unexpected direction, the natural reaction from other mathematicians is skepticism. That's healthy. Mathematics has a long history of beautiful conjectures that turned out to be false, and of "proofs" that had subtle gaps. So the proof is the common language that lets a stranger's idea enter the shared body of knowledge. You don't have to know the person, trust their reputation, or share their intuition. If the argument is there and each step checks out, you have to accept it.

But in practice it's more nuanced than that. A proof also has to be *readable* by the community. Historically there are cases where someone had a correct idea but expressed it in a framework nobody else understood yet, and acceptance took years, sometimes decades, because people had to build the bridges to verify it. Think of how long it can take for a very long or very novel proof to be digested by experts. Correctness alone isn't sufficient for acceptance. You also need people who can follow it, who can see why it works, and ideally who can reuse the techniques.

That's part of why I'm excited about formal verification and tools like Lean. They change the social dynamics of trust. If a proof is formally verified, the question "is this correct?" is separated from the question "do I understand it?" That's powerful, especially as AI systems start producing mathematics. An AI might generate an argument that's very unfamiliar in style, and a human referee might not want to spend months checking it. A machine-checked proof gives you a foundation of certainty, and then the human work can shift toward understanding, interpreting, and building on it.

So for me, proof is the mechanism that turns a private insight into public knowledge. And the more unfamiliar the discovery, the more important it is that the proof be both rigorous and, eventually, explainable, because acceptance in mathematics is ultimately about the community being able to stand on that result and go further.

r001.rationale: The response discusses proof as a common language and community skepticism, but does not say shared mathematical training fosters shared intuitions about what claims should naturally be true.

r002.rationale: It says proof lets a stranger’s idea enter shared mathematical knowledge and that mathematicians can accept it when each step checks out.

r003.rationale: It separates correctness from understanding and readability, but does not distinguish acceptance of correctness from a later judgment of the proof’s beauty or naturalness.

fable-5.1.text:
I think proof is the thing that makes mathematics unusual among all the ways humans try to persuade each other. In most fields, if you show up with a claim nobody has heard before, you have to fight on two fronts: whether the claim is true, and whether anyone trusts you enough to check. In math, proof collapses those into one. It's a kind of protocol that lets a stranger verify your discovery without needing to know who you are, where you trained, or whether your intuition is any good.

That matters a lot for unfamiliar ideas specifically. When something is new, people's instincts are usually against it. The intuitions of a whole community have been trained on the old picture, so a new object or a new connection feels wrong before it feels right. If acceptance depended on intuition, the unfamiliar thing would lose almost every time. Proof is what lets it win anyway. You can say, "I know this feels strange, but here is a chain of steps, and each step you already accept." It forces engagement on the merits.

But I'd also say proof is necessary and not sufficient. A correct proof of something nobody cares about doesn't travel. What actually gets a discovery absorbed is when the proof teaches people something. The best proofs don't just certify a statement, they reorganize how you see the surrounding landscape, so that afterward the result looks almost inevitable. Mathematicians often talk about a proof being "the right proof," and that's what they mean. The first proof of something unfamiliar is often ugly and defensive, built to survive scrutiny. Then over years the community finds cleaner proofs, and that's really the process of the idea becoming familiar.

And there's a social layer that people underestimate. Proofs are read by humans, and humans have finite patience. A long, technical argument from someone outside the mainstream might be correct and still sit unread for a long time. So part of the role of proof is communication: structuring the argument so that someone with the standard background can get traction, isolating the one genuinely new idea so a reader can test it in their own mind. When that works, the proof isn't just a certificate. It's an invitation, and the community takes it up because they can see where the door is.

So I'd put it this way: proof is what makes it possible for an unfamiliar discovery to be accepted at all, and good proof is what makes it actually happen.

r001.rationale: The response says a community’s intuitions are trained on the old picture, but does not state that shared mathematical training creates shared intuitions about what claims should naturally be true.

r002.rationale: It describes proof as a protocol that lets a stranger verify a discovery without relying on the discoverer’s identity, and says proof lets an unfamiliar idea win on its merits.

r003.rationale: It separates a proof’s correctness from its explanatory and aesthetic value: a correct proof may not travel, while later cleaner proofs can make the idea familiar.

astra-6.text:
I think proof gives mathematicians a way to evaluate an unfamiliar idea without having to share the intuition that led to it. You might arrive at a discovery through examples, or a pattern, or a connection that feels very surprising. But for someone else, that feeling isn’t enough. A proof lets them follow the reasoning and check whether the conclusion really follows from the assumptions.

There’s also a distinction between convincing someone that a result is true and helping them understand why it’s true. A proof can do both, but sometimes the first proof establishes the result, and later proofs make the underlying structure clearer. So I see proof as both a standard of justification and a means of communication. It turns an individual insight into something the mathematical community can examine, use, and build on.

r001.rationale: The response says proof lets others assess an idea without sharing its originating intuition, but does not state that shared mathematical training creates shared intuitions about what claims should naturally be true.

r002.rationale: It presents proof as a way for others to check and examine a result, but does not identify mathematicians outside an established community gaining that community’s acceptance.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes establishing that a result is true from understanding why it is true, but does not discuss judging the beauty or naturalness of a proof.

sol-6.1.text:
I think proof gives mathematicians a shared way to evaluate an unfamiliar idea. You might arrive at a discovery through intuition, examples, or a connection that initially seems surprising, but those things alone don’t establish that it’s true. A proof lets someone else follow the argument and check it independently, even if their intuition is very different from yours.

But there’s also a distinction between convincing someone that a result is true and helping them understand why it’s true. A good proof can do both. It makes the discovery rigorous, while also revealing the structure behind it—so that other mathematicians can build on the idea.

r001.rationale: It describes proof as a shared way to evaluate ideas, but does not say shared mathematical training fosters shared intuitions about which claims should naturally be true.

r002.rationale: It says proof lets someone independently check an unfamiliar idea, but does not identify outsiders to an established mathematical community or community acceptance.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes establishing truth from helping others understand why, but does not distinguish correctness from later judging a proof’s beauty or naturalness.
